text: Notebooks are ideal for exploring. But once your cleaning logic works, leaving it buried in cell 47 has real costs: you can't test it, you can't run it on a schedule, and two people can't easily edit it at once. Refactoring means moving the reusable parts into plain Python files, while keeping the notebook for what it does best — exploring and presenting.

A useful rule of thumb: anything you'd want to run twice, or test, moves out. That's usually the loading, cleaning, and feature-building steps. What stays in the notebook is the exploration, the charts, and the narrative explaining what you found. The path has four steps: get the notebook working top to bottom, turn important cells into functions, move those functions into a dot p y module, then add a script that wires them together.

A simple project layout: a data folder for the raw file, a package folder — orders underscore pipeline — containing an empty init file plus cleaning dot p y, a run underscore pipeline dot p y script, and the analysis notebook. The empty init file is what marks orders underscore pipeline as an importable package.

Inside cleaning dot p y, each small function does one job and returns a new DataFrame: standardize underscore region trims whitespace and title-cases the column, add underscore revenue multiplies quantity by unit price. clean underscore orders chains them together with dot pipe, which passes the DataFrame into each function in turn — dedupe, standardize, add revenue.

run underscore pipeline dot p y wires it together with two ideas worth naming. argparse turns command-line flags into a tidy args object, so file paths aren't hard-coded. And if underscore underscore name underscore underscore equals equals quote main quote means 'only run main when this file is executed directly' — importing it elsewhere won't trigger it. Using pathlib dot Path keeps the code working on Windows, macOS, and Linux.

Run it from the project folder with python run_pipeline.py, an --input flag, and an --output flag. With our five-row sample containing one duplicate order, it prints: read 5 rows, wrote 4 rows. The output file has cleaned regions — North, South, East — and a revenue column.

Back in the notebook, one cell replaces dozens: import clean underscore orders from the module, and call it on the raw CSV. This works when the notebook runs from the project folder. If you keep editing the module while the notebook is open, the IPython magics load underscore ext autoreload and autoreload 2 reload your changes automatically — no restart needed.

To recap: move anything you'd rerun or test into functions, then into a module. Keep exploration, charts, and commentary in the notebook. A script with main, argparse, and the dunder-main guard is repeatable and schedulable. Use pathlib and arguments instead of hard-coded paths. Next, we protect this code with automated tests.
